questions.q: What does a quantum backend actually return after executing a circuit for N shots?
options: A dictionary of measured bitstring counts (e.g., {"0": 612, "1": 388}) and the shot count -- not a single final answer
The optimal parameters for the next iteration of the loop
A ready-to-use probability distribution with standard error pre-attached
A single floating-point expectation value, already computed
questions.explain: Backends return raw measurement counts per bitstring plus the total shot count. Converting that into an expectation value, with its standard error, is classical post-processing code the engineer writes.

questions.q: Given counts {"0": 612, "1": 388} over 1,000 shots with the convention |0> -> +1, |1> -> -1, what is <Z>?
options: -0.224, because |1> is the dominant convention
0.612, equal to the fraction of 0 outcomes
1.0, since |0> always maps to +1
questions.explain: <Z> is the counts-weighted average of the eigenvalues: (612x(+1) + 388x(-1))/1000 = 224/1000 = 0.224.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist on reporting an expectation value together with its standard error (e.g., 0.224 +/- 0.032) rather than the bare number?
options: Standard error changes the actual value of the expectation value
The bare expectation value is always wrong without a standard error correction applied first

Without the standard error attached, it's easy to mistake a difference between two results that's smaller than the noise floor for a real, meaningful difference -- the same error flagged as Mistake 4 in the previous chapter
Standard error is required by cloud providers' billing systems
questions.explain: Reporting the standard error lets anyone consuming the number judge whether an observed difference between two results is statistically meaningful or just shot noise -- omitting it invites exactly the shot-noise misinterpretation covered in the previous lesson's Mistake 4.

questions.q: When aggregating results from a 100-circuit program set where shot counts differ per circuit (e.g., due to a partial retry), what is the correct way to combine them into one expectation value?
options: Multiply each circuit's expectation value by its circuit index
Average each circuit's individual expectation value with equal weight, regardless of how many shots each circuit ran
Use only the circuit with the most shots and discard the rest

Weight each circuit's contribution by its actual shot count: sum of (counts[0]-counts[1]) across circuits, divided by the sum of shots across circuits -- not a simple average of each circuit's individual expectation value
questions.explain: A simple equal-weighted average over-weights low-shot (noisier) circuits the same as high-shot ones. Shot-weighted aggregation correctly reflects each circuit's actual statistical contribution.

questions.q: Which of these is listed in the lesson as an easy-to-ship post-processing bug?
options: Assuming the wrong eigenvalue convention for a measurement basis, which silently flips the sign of every downstream result with no error thrown
The QPU returning a negative shot count
The optimizer refusing to accept any expectation value below zero
Cloud providers refusing to return measurement counts at all
questions.explain: A sign/basis convention error (e.g., assuming |0>->-1 instead of +1) silently flips every downstream value without throwing any error -- exactly the kind of bug that unit tests against known-answer counts dictionaries are meant to catch.
